maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF LEADER OF TANGANYIKA NATIONAL UNION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF LEADER OF TANGANYIKA NATIONAL UNION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by leave of the house I should like to mention the fact that present in the Speaker's gallery today is Mr. Julius K. Nyerere the distinguished leader of the Tanganyika African National Union. This distinguished statesman from Africa has recently completed a speaking tour of the United States under the auspices of the state department, and those who were privileged to hear him speak today at the Canadian Club realize the power and capacity of our visitor.
We are happy that he has been able to spend this short time in Ottawa, and on his return to Tanganyika-I am sure I speak for hon. members in all parts of the house-we wish him to convey to his people the greetings of the Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF LEADER OF TANGANYIKA NATIONAL UNION
speechtext: I should like to associate our party with the words of welcome which the Prime Minister has just uttered to our distinguished visitor. All Canadians are following the progress of the African peoples to independence under law with sympathy and support; especially, if I may say so, with regard to those peoples who have been under British colonial rule and who, when they achieve independence, will we hope become nations within the British commonwealth.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF LEADER OF TANGANYIKA NATIONAL UNION
speechtext: I should like to add on behalf of the C.C.F. party our word of welcome to our distinguished guest. 1 think one of the most hopeful developments in the world today is the emergence of independent free nations in Africa. I associate myself with the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in heartily welcoming our guest and looking forward to the development of Tanganyika within the commonwealth of nations.

subtopic: JACQUES CARTIER BRIDGE, MONTREAL-REQUEST THAT COMMITTEE RESUME SITTINGS

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: JACQUES CARTIER BRIDGE, MONTREAL-REQUEST THAT COMMITTEE RESUME SITTINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, February 24 last, I advised the house that the investigation into possible criminal activities
in connection with the collection of tolls on Jacques Cartier bridge had advanced to the point where it appeared that criminal charges should be laid, and that accordingly the Minister of Justice had appointed counsel to assess the evidence, to advise as to the course of further criminal investigations, and to draft charges that should be laid. At the same time I announced that as soon as charges had been laid the government would ask the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines to resume its hearings immediately and make the fullest possible examination of all other aspects of the matter.
The Minister of Justice has now been advised that it may take considerably longer than was first anticipated to bring the matter before the courts because of the time and care that must be taken in the weighing of the evidence. The government is therefore of the view that the hearings of the committee to examine other aspects of the situation should not be indefinitely delayed, and has asked that the committee be called to meet for that purpose on Monday morning next, March 14.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF AGREEMENT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: EXTENSION OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I wonder whether the minister could report further to

Inquiries of the Ministry the house on the progress of the Canadian-U.S.S.R. trade agreement. Would the minister care to comment on a statement in this morning's Globe and Mail to the effect that an agreement is about to be signed which is to cover the annual purchase by Russia of some 15 million bushels of wheat from Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: EXTENSION OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we are all very much interested in this particular matter, and all are hopeful that a trade agreement with Russia can be signed. The negotiations have been proceeding for over a year, and they have not been without some difficulties.
We have been endeavouring to secure a basis for trade which would provide for adequate sales of Canadian goods and products including wheat in the Soviet union, which is a state trading country, and in return we would offer, as was done in the past, most favoured nation treatment for Soviet goods entering the open Canadian market.
A number of possibilities have been carefully examined by both sides. In recent months proposals have been made to us by the U.S.S.R. including as one element the offer, subject to certain conditions, to exchange goods on a 2 to 1 basis in Canada's favour. We have considered these proposals and made our reply, and now await the reaction of the Soviet government. I consider that we are now close to an understanding, and again I express the hope that the matter will be brought to a conclusion very quickly.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question. Do I take it from the minister's reply that Canada is prepared to make some kind of commitment to buy from the Soviet union at least 50 per cent of the value of the goods she buys from us?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: EXTENSION OF AGREEMENT
speechtext: No, the Canadian government cannot make a commitment as a government to buy from Russia. Russia is a state trading nation and we are not, and that makes quite a difference.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF AGREEMENT
speechtext: A further supplementary question. Is any assurance of any kind being given the Soviet union that Canada's importers will be buying up to this proportion of goods from the Soviet union?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: EXTENSION OF AGREEMENT
speechtext: It is very difficult to give an assurance of that nature, Mr. Speaker, because it would be up to Canadian businessmen, using their own good judgment, as to what they import into this country.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

The minister was kind enough on February 3 in answer to a question of mine to say that the discussions with the Soviet union with regard to this treaty did not include a particular model of automobile manufactured in the Soviet union and known as the Mosk-vich 407. The minister said in reply to my question that the discussions did not include the importation or the inclusion of that particular automobile in the proposed treaty.
May I ask the minister now whether any type of Russian-made automobile forms one of the subjects of discussion between the two negotiating bodies.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: EXTENSION OF AGREEMENT
speechtext: Not to my knowledge, Mr. Speaker. Specific items like that have not been brought to my attention.

maintopic: REPORTED RECORD DEFICIT IN INTERNATIONAL PAYMENTS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REPORTED RECORD DEFICIT IN INTERNATIONAL PAYMENTS
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce based on the daily bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics of today, which reports an all-time record deficit for 1959 in Canada's international payments. Does the minister propose to make a statement to the house concerning the serious situation disclosed by the bulletin, and does he propose to bring before the house this session any legislation specifically dealing with this subject?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REPORTED RECORD DEFICIT IN INTERNATIONAL PAYMENTS
speechtext: I do not consider the situation anything like as serious as has been suggested by the hon. member. The daily bulletin has drawn our attention to what it calls a record deficit in 1959 on Canada's international payments. For 1959 as a whole merchandise exports increased by 5 per cent whereas imports rose by 9 per cent compared with 1958, and that increase is reflected in the balance figures for 1959. In the last three months exports have risen by 17 per cent and imports by only 5 per cent from the corresponding period a year ago. In other words the rise in the current deficit which occurred in 1959 is not being sustained into 1960, whereas Canada's foreign earnings are rising sharply.

maintopic: REPORTED RECORD DEFICIT IN INTERNATIONAL PAYMENTS
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. When the minister uses the term "Canada's foreign earnings" at the conclusion of his remarks, is he referring to foreign earnings arising out of commodity trade or foreign earnings generally?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REPORTED RECORD DEFICIT IN INTERNATIONAL PAYMENTS
speechtext: In particular with regard to trade, commodity trade.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DIVISION OF MINISTERIAL RESPONSIBILITY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DIVISION OF MINISTERIAL RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. In order to avoid the misdirection of office missives and orders of the day missiles aimed at the outer space of the Department of National Defence, and to avoid any consequent misfiring or backfiring, would the minister be kind enough to inform the house as to the recent division of responsibilities between himself and his associate minister?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DIVISION OF MINISTERIAL RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: Before the minister answers, I raise the question as to whether this is not a matter of statutory interpretation. I cannot say from memory; perhaps some member of the house can assist me in this. My recollection is that the joint or associate ministry is established by a statute of parliament. If this is so perhaps the question is one for interpretation of one of our acts of parliament, which it is not customary to ask on orders of the day.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DIVISION OF MINISTERIAL RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, while it is true that the post is established by statute, I believe in this case there was some directive or other document from the Prime Minister or from the office of the privy council setting out the specific duties of the two ministers. I think the question is quite in order, and that it would be useful for the house to know what the division of responsibility is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DIVISION OF MINISTERIAL RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: What kind of directive did you have?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DIVISION OF MINISTERIAL RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, surely the matter still falls to be dealt with in accordance with the principle to which you have directed our attention, that any answer to the hon. member's question would be a matter for interpretation, not a matter to be answered on the orders of the day. Any such directive would speak for itself.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DIVISION OF MINISTERIAL RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if there is a directive I submit that under the doctrine of responsible government, under which we operate in this house, it ought to be laid before the house so we may know which minister is responsible for which part of the administration. To the best of my recollection no such directive has been laid before the house. My recollection is that when my hon. friend from Trinity was the associate minister, and when
Inquiries of the Ministry his predecessor Mr. Campney was the associate minister, and when Mr. Power was an associate minister, a very clear definition of functions was given to the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DIVISION OF MINISTERIAL RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: If it is a matter of record and the information can be obtained from the statute or the record, then of course it is open to any member of the house to get the information for himself. Since there is some doubt, perhaps the minister might assist in clearing it up.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DIVISION OF MINISTERIAL RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: No specific directive has been issued as to the duties, but by mutual agreement between the associate minister and myself, in general terms we consult on all matters affecting the department, but more particularly, the minister of defence deals with matters of policy while the associate minister deals with administration, particularly those matters which refer to personnel, both military and civilian. However, if the hon. member's missiles are not equipped with a homing warhead, I will see that they reach the right target.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DIVISION OF MINISTERIAL RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the minister's reply has been very helpful, and that in future the opposition should address all questions of policy to the minister and all questions of administration to the associate minister.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DIVISION OF MINISTERIAL RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the instructions issued to the hon. member for Trinity when he was associate minister were simply to keep out of the way as much as possible?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DIVISION OF MINISTERIAL RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: A supplementary question. How does the minister explain that every time there is an important meeting with the military authorities the Minister of National Defence is always alone and the associate minister is never there?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DIVISION OF MINISTERIAL RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext: That is absolutely incorrect. Whenever there are any matters of policy discussed with the chief of the general staff or with the chiefs of the other services, the associate minister is always present.

subtopic: P.G.E. RAILWAY-FEDERAL SUBSIDY PAYMENTS ALLEGED OWING TO BRITISH COLUMBIA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: P.G.E. RAILWAY-FEDERAL SUBSIDY PAYMENTS ALLEGED OWING TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Has the Prime Minister noted the claim of the premier of British Columbia to the effect that Ottawa owes British Columbia $13 million in subsidy payments on the Pacific Great Eastern Railway? Has the government of British Columbia ever made application for this amount of money and, if it has, can the Prime Minister indicate what has been the decision of the government in this regard?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: P.G.E. RAILWAY-FEDERAL SUBSIDY PAYMENTS ALLEGED OWING TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have noted the press reference which the hon. member sent to me. An agreement was entered into for payment of a federal subsidy for a specified portion of construction of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway immediately north of Prince George. Payment of the federal funds owing under this agreement has been made. Although the fact is that the provincial government has at various times requested additional subsidies for additional construction, there is no record that any further agreement in this connection was made by the former administration, and I know of no such further agreement having been made by the present administration. There were references made to this matter on one or two occasions, but as far as the government is concerned there is nothing to indicate that any amount is owing to the province of British Columbia.

maintopic: REPORTED REMARKS BY MINISTER OF JUSTICE ON NARCOTIC CONTROL

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REPORTED REMARKS BY MINISTER OF JUSTICE ON NARCOTIC CONTROL
speechtext:
May I ask
a question of the Minister of Justice, and in doing so may I preface my query by congratulating him on his birthday today. Will the minister tell the house whether he has in mind certain proposals, which he is reported to have indicated to the provinces he was prepared to make, for the more efficient operation of narcotic drug control? Could he inform the house what these proposals are?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fullon (Minisler of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REPORTED REMARKS BY MINISTER OF JUSTICE ON NARCOTIC CONTROL
speechtext:
thank the hon. gentleman, indeed, for his kind reference to my birthday, and in the

light of the mood which he has produced I shall endeavour to answer his question. I think he bases it on the report of a comment I made in Victoria recently when I was out there in the course of the Columbia river negotiation, at which time I pointed out that with the full knowledge and consent of my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the question of drug addiction in Canada had been referred to the correctional planning committee of my department, with respect primarily of course to the criminal aspect of addiction. I said at that time that the committee had reached certain tentative conclusions which have been submitted to myself and my colleague, and that I expected shortly to be in a position to lay these before my colleagues in the cabinet, and that thereafter it might well be we would have proposals to make to the provinces.

maintopic: REPORTED REMARKS BY MINISTER OF JUSTICE ON NARCOTIC CONTROL
speechtext: Would that be this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REPORTED REMARKS BY MINISTER OF JUSTICE ON NARCOTIC CONTROL
speechtext: That I am not able to say, Mr. Speaker. The matter is a difficult and complicated one, and it depends upon the rate of progress that we are able to make.

subtopic: POSSIBLE THEFT OF MAIL FROM MOTOR SCOOTERS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: POSSIBLE THEFT OF MAIL FROM MOTOR SCOOTERS
speechtext:
May I ask
a question of the Postmaster General. In yesterday's newspaper there are pictures of a postman returning to his scooter after delivering mail to an apartment house. It looks as if the scooter has been left alone on the street without any protection from theft, and with the doors wide open to the 500 pounds of mail which it might be carrying. Will the minister tell the house whether this is a new method the government has adopted for protection against theft?

subtopic: POSSIBLE THEFT OF MAIL FROM MOTOR SCOOTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the scooters we use have the mail completely protected in the back part of the vehicle, with locked doors. The hon. member was looking at the front portion, which is the driver's compartment, and which is quite separate from the part of the body in which the mail is carried. I might say, Mr. Speaker, that I would be delighted to arrange for the hon. member to come down to the Ottawa terminal and personally inspect one of these scooters.

subtopic: POSSIBLE THEFT OF MAIL FROM MOTOR SCOOTERS
speechtext:
May I ask a supplementary question. The minister knows that recently a truck was stolen with the driver in it. I should like to know whether the motor of the
Inquiries of the Ministry scooter is kept running, or whether the postman has to start the motor again every time he makes a delivery.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: POSSIBLE THEFT OF MAIL FROM MOTOR SCOOTERS
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is getting too theoretical and hypothetical. Perhaps the hon. member will accept the invitation to go and examine the scooter.

subtopic: POSSIBLE THEFT OF MAIL FROM MOTOR SCOOTERS
speechtext: How does the minister explain that the ordinary postman is obliged to carry his load in a bag up to the fourth or fifth floor and has to keep it with him, while the scooter with mail is left in the street unprotected?

subtopic: POSSIBLE THEFT OF MAIL FROM MOTOR SCOOTERS
speechtext: There are few people in Canada capable of carrying away 500 pounds of mail plus the scooter.

subtopic: POSSIBLE THEFT OF MAIL FROM MOTOR SCOOTERS
speechtext: I do not suggest that the postman should climb up with the scooter on his back.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: POSSIBLE THEFT OF MAIL FROM MOTOR SCOOTERS
speechtext: Order. The question in my mind is whether the subject will be exhausted before the house is.

subtopic: POSSIBLE THEFT OF MAIL FROM MOTOR SCOOTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: POSSIBLE THEFT OF MAIL FROM MOTOR SCOOTERS
speechtext: The hon. member has asked his supplementary question.

subtopic: POSSIBLE THEFT OF MAIL FROM MOTOR SCOOTERS
speechtext: I have another question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: POSSIBLE THEFT OF MAIL FROM MOTOR SCOOTERS
speechtext: I misunderstood the hon. member. I thought he had the same piece of paper in his hand.

subtopic: POSSIBLE THEFT OF MAIL FROM MOTOR SCOOTERS
speechtext: No; it is another picture showing a scooter and the Postmaster General. I should like to know from the Postmaster General which of the two is the main feature.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS RIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, March 9, consideration of the motion of Mrs. Fair dough for the second reading of Bill No. C-2, to amend the Indian Act.
Indian Act

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS RIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was saying when I was interrupted yesterday that citizens' committees in various communities where our Indian citizens reside are most important in assisting the Indian affairs branch in carrying out their functions. I may say that while the federal government has a definite responsibility so far as Indian welfare is concerned, it is of the utmost importance to recognize, all along the line, that the Indian people are citizens of the provinces, of the territories and of the communities in which they reside. Acceptance of them as such by all levels of government and by all other citizens is an essential factor in their integration.
I would draw a very definite line, as many hon. members have done in debates on this subject in the past, between the integration of the Indian people and the assimilation of these people. This is why it is so important that the amendment now before the house should be couched' in its present terms, giving a choice to the Indian people so that if they do not wish to vote they need not vote, and whether they vote or do not vote they lose none of their rights.
The federal government alone cannot fully discharge the whole of the responsibility. Each level of government, each voluntary association, each individual citizen must play a part if success is to be expected. The aim of the government would, in my view, fail regrettably if the Indian people of Canada were not brought to the point at which they could, if they wished, take their place in the community as citizens in all respects, to the same extent as any hon. member of this house, having the same rights and assuming the same responsibilities as all other citizens without discrimination or distinction of any kind.
Here I disagree with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate as to the acceptance of the Indian people by other Canadians as fully fledged citizens. I do not think there is that acceptance, or that there has been such acceptance for many years. We may pay lip service to the idea of accepting Indians as fellow citizens, but government at all levels, as far as my experience goes, has yet to recognize the Indians as citizens equal in all respects to their white counterparts.
Under the treaties themselves the Indians obtained a legal status inferior to our own. Under the Indian Act as it existed in the past the legal status of Indians was in my view reduced even further. The Indian Act which was passed in 1868 has not been improved to any great extent. While I do not propose to review the terms of the act, even if it were in order to do so, I wish to consider some aspects of the present act in so far as they

Indian Act
relate to the bill under discussion. Undoubtedly, in the past, some special legislation was required in order to protect the Indian. Nowadays, however, thousands of Indians are able to take advantage of the experience gained while they were in Europe during the last world war. They can read, they can write, and they have radios. In short, they now know that they live in a democracy, and they would like some of the benefits of that democracy themselves.
I am speaking now of the Indian people I know best, those people who live in the Yukon and in the north. Hopes ran high among the Indian people in those regions- and I believe they also ran high among the Indian people living in the more southerly areas of Canada-when they heard that they were at last to get a new Indian Act. That was a few years ago, in 1951 or 1952, I believe. They hoped at that time that they would get the vote, despite what the former minister said in 1951 to the effect that this was not anticipated by the majority of the Indian people. Nevertheless it is my belief that the Indian people did hope they would get the vote and be able to run their own affairs.
Some advantages were given to them by the new act, but Indian affairs continue to be run in most cases in the same manner as they were 90 years ago. The new act really did not give the Indians the vote. The courts have held that Indian property, both real and personal, off the reserve is taxable, but that on the reserve it is not. Under the Indian Act as it now stands the Indian, if he takes the vote, will be taxed on his land and personal property on the reserve, and must in addition pay succession and inheritance taxes. The Indian can now, with the consent of the minister, apply for enfranchisement, become a Canadian citizen and then have the vote, but he must transfer his land to another Indian on the reserve within 30 days and sell any improvement he may have made on it. If it is not sold within that period the land is auctioned off, and he must take what he can get for it. Once enfranchised, neither he nor his wife nor his children can ever return to the reserve. They receive compensation for the income they would have received had they stayed on the reserve for the next 20 years, but of course this is much less than the children would have eventually received.
These terms make the Indian people dread the process of enfranchisement, as distinguished from the right to vote. To them it is a threat rather than a privilege, and the section in the act which allows an individual or a whole tribe to be forced into enfranchisement without consent-section 112, to

which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate was referring-is truly a threat over the heads of the Indian people. It is difficult for an Indian to give up his only home and the only way of life he knows before he can receive the privilege of the vote; that is, under the process of enfranchisement.

speechtext: The hon. member mentioned my name, and I did not hear what he said about section 112. I was very interested in what he was saying, but there was a noise and I could not hear it.

speechtext: From my recollection of the remarks made by the hon. member yesterday I took it that he was advocating the repeal of section 112.

speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS RIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext:
In this I am agreeing with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, because I say this is truly a very real threat which hangs over the heads of the Indian people today. I was saying that it is difficult for an Indian to give up his only home and the only way of life he knows just to receive the privilege of voting under the process which section 112 allows. With his limited experience he usually feels the price is too high. He cannot foresee that without the vote he will never have a voice in running his own affairs or enacting the laws which govern him.
Not only is it extremely difficult for the Indian to obtain the vote, but he also lacks that fundamental right we all cherish so, the right to own property. Off the reserve the Indian may own property, but on the reserve he may not. It matters not whether the title for the reserve is held in the name of the crown or whether it is a grant; as long as the property is for the exclusive use of the Indians it is under the jurisdiction of the department of Indian affairs, and from their decision there is no appeal. The minister of the department may decide what the reserve will be used for, that is what portion will be divided into lots or sections, or whether it will be divided at all. She may decide where the roads shall run and what portion will be set aside for schools and hospitals. No Indian may hold even a small portion of his own reserve as his own. If the tribe votes a portion of the reserve to any one Indian the minister may, if she so desires, take the land from that Indian and give it to another.
I am pointing out these distinctions to give emphasis to my disagreement with the statement made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that there exists an equality of citizenship, because it is a far cry from equality. I am pointing out these distinctions to my hon. friend to show that there is

indeed a very wide gap between citizenship for the white person and citizenship for the Indian person in Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS RIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext: Does the hon. member think that in saying this he is disagreeing with me? I could not agree more. I feel we should remove that gap.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS RIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext: I took it from my hon. friend's remarks yesterday that he suggested there was an equality of citizenship. I made a note of his remarks. In speaking on the resolution my hon. friend said that the Indian people are Canadian citizens like all other Canadian citizens.

speechtext: That is true.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS RIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext: We may be paying lip service to that ideal but it is not true in fact. In speaking on the bill my hon. friend said that the status of the Indian person was no different from that of an ordinary person. Theoretically that may be so, but in fact it is far from true.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS RIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman would permit me to clarify that. I was thinking of the status of an Indian under the citizenship act. I think perhaps in a broader sense the hon. member may be quite right in what he says.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS RIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext:
If the minister does take the land of an Indian she will pay the Indian the amount she decides for the house and any improvements he has made on that land. Even on the Indian's death his widow cannot stay on the land unless the minister consents to her presence, nor can the Indian's heirs remain on the land. The Indian cannot lease any portion of the land the tribe may have voted him without the minister's consent. He may, with the consent of the minister and of the whole tribe, surrender his land back to the crown and the minister may then dispose of that land in the manner in which she sees fit.
If the whole tribe desire to leave the reserve they cannot sell their reserve without the minister's consent. The department may even lease the Indian's land to a white man, if it so desires, for one year without the Indian's consent. In the act there is a section which says the tribes or bands may, if they get the government's consent, obtain control of the land on their own reserve and supervise its allotment; but as this consent can be withdrawn at any time it offers little hope to the Indian of ever getting permanent control of his property. The fact that the Indian must always be a tenant of the crown discourages him from improving his land or taking pride in it. In other words, the
Indian Act
minister of the department has complete control of all the Indians' land. The Indian, because he has no vote, has no real voice in the appointment of the minister, and from the minister's decision there is no appeal.
It may be of interest to the house to note that no transfer of property on the reserve is valid without the minister's consent; and this includes minerals, gravel, timber and oil; and that no property on the reserve-and this includes property bought with band funds-may be mortgaged or attached, and no order for seizure or execution of such property is valid, unless it is a chattel sold to an Indian under a conditional sales agreement. In the latter case the chattel can be redeemed.
Not only does the Indian not have any control over his real property, but in Alberta and Saskatchewan no Indian may sell or exchange either crops or cattle or anything he produces unless he first obtains the consent of the department. The Indians of the west hate this section. It is discouraging to get half way through the deal to sell your hay and then have to go 20 miles to find the agent and get his consent before you can complete the deal; and if the Indian agent refuses his consent there is nothing the Indian can do about it.
As to the question of the Indian's control over his money, any money an individual Indian has acquired is his own to spend on what he may want. Money that belongs to the tribe as a whole is known as band funds. There are no such band funds in the Yukon, even though there are bands. Indeed, there is no property upon which the Yukon Indian people could build up such funds, because they have no right to any of the land, there never having been a treaty negotiated with the Indian people of the Yukon, a lack which I sincerely trust will soon be remedied.
With respect to the band fund, the portion of this fund that is derived from the sale of surrendered land or capital assets such as oil, gravel, timber, etc., is called the capital fund, while the portion derived from the selling of jointly owned produce, leases, etc., is known as the revenue fund. This money is the Indians', and the department cannot spend it without the consent of the Indian council. However, many of the Indians feel bitter that they cannot make the department spend their money for the things they desire, such as hospitals, etc. If the department thinks them unnecessary the tribe cannot spend its own money on them. The only cash the Indian may actually receive from his band fund is under the new act, under which the department can, with the Indians'

Indian Act
consent, pay out 50 per cent of the capital fund to the Indians on a per capita basis. This is being done on oil rich reserves; otherwise the Indian receives none of the band fund as his own, nor can he compel the department to spend this fund in the manner in which he desires.
In the matter of electing their own chiefs, the Indians may with, the consent of the governor in council, elect a chief and an Indian council, but the election is at the option of the governor general in council and at his discretion. The council do not, unless the minister allows it, actually run the business of the reserve. They cannot pass money by-laws but only by-laws regarding relatively unimportant matters, and these can only be enforced if they are approved by the minister.
The department has complete jurisdiction as to schools, infants, and mental deficients on the reserve and it has complete jurisdiction as to all matters pertaining to an Indian's will. The courts may only exercise jurisdiction in an Indian's will with the minister's consent, and can make no order as to real property without his consent. The minister alone can grant probate or declare the will void. There is no appeal from the minister's decision in this matter unless the estate is over $500; and since the Indian does not own his own land, and most of his money is in the band fund, this is an exceptional case. If, however, the estate is over $500 the Indian may appeal the minister's decision to a court if the minister allows him to appeal.

speechtext:
Order. Would the hon.
member permit me to ask him how he relates all these interesting facts to the bill itself which, as I understand it, is for the simple purpose of giving the vote to Indians? He may find it necessary to lay a background, I admit, but it seems to me that in dealing generally with the problems of Indians the hon. member is going beyond the principle on second reading of the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS RIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped
that I was not dealing generally with the problems of the Indian people but rather with the method of administration of Indian affairs by the department. I was attempting to show that this method of administration is one of the real reasons why Indian peoples should have to vote, so they may have some part in saying how these various things should be done.
I might simply conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that under the Indian Act the Indian definitely has a legal status inferior to that of the average Canadian. Nearly every aspect of his life is subject to the discretion

or consent of either the Indian affairs branch, the cabinet or the minister, and in neither case can he have a voice in their appointment or election at the present time.
In all fairness to the government this dictatorship that is imposed by the government is done for the Indian's protection, and it has been so for the past 90 years now. If the discretionary powers of the department were removed some of the poorer and less educated reserves could possibly destroy their assets. The more advanced and better type Indian, however, is being held back by not being allowed to handle his own affairs.
It is obvious that if the department acts truly in the best interests of the Indian, no harm can come to him just because the department has the right to control all his activities. However, the fact remains that if the department chooses to not act in the Indian's better interests, a great injustice can be done; and at present the Indian can do nothing to protect himself from this injustice, as there is no appeal from the minister's decision. The question is, how can the department protect the Indian and yet the Indian still enjoy individual freedom and liberty? One of the quickest methods I can see, Mr. Speaker, to accomplish this is by the house giving assent to the bill before us.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS RIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext: Might I rise to take issue with a statement made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, in the part of his speech made last evening?

On this point I am afraid X am in disagreement with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) because it is not up to us to impose our own views and our own standards upon the Indian people.
Well, sir, I never said and I hope I never implied that I thought we ought to impose our own views and our own standards upon them. I have always taken exactly the contrary view, and in that regard I think I agree with the hon. gentleman and he agrees with me.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS RIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext: I had no intention to impute such motives to the hon. gentleman.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS RIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in past sessions I have had occasion to introduce bills similar in design and intent to the one we are discussing at the moment and the one which follows it. I am quite pleased to be able to express appreciation

and thanks to the minister for having indicated that this is the government's intention also, and naturally they will have a much better chance to pass now that the minister is responsible for the bills than they did when I introduced the same things on two or three occasions in the past.
I am very pleased to see this action being taken at the present time. I am sure that even though there are indications of opposition to it in some sections of the Indian population, as time passes the Indians will realize that there are beneficial things which are accruing to them from having been given the vote.
I regret that as an elected member I have to vote on such a question as this. I regret it only because I think it should have been done by the Liberal party when it was in office many years ago, and the right to vote should not have been cluttered up with taxation exemption waivers as was done in 1951 or 1952. It has always been my thought that there should be no impediments, no restrictions, no strings attached to the right not only of our Indian population but of anybody else in Canada to vote. That right in Canada should be inviolate and completely free.
There is a fear, certainly, and mistrust in some sections of the Indian population. This fear should be removed. I know the Prime Minister has said it; the minister has said it, and all of us who are familiar with the contents of these two bills have said it is a fact that no treaty, aboriginal or hereditary rights are infringed upon, and there is no connection between the right to vote and those particular rights in so far as infringement is concerned. But I still think it would be well for the minister to consider accepting the suggestion made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate yesterday, which had to do with the section which was contained in the bills I introduced two or three sessions ago; namely that in the act itself, which parliament enacts, it should be made clear by a separate section, or a subsection attached to it, that this is in no way an infringement upon or a detraction from the hereditary, aboriginal or treaty rights of Indians, so that in reading the Indian Act or the proposed amendments, when they are passed and become part of the law of the nation, the Indians will see that in the legislation it is specifically spelled out that there is no attempt to infringe upon those rights.
The Indian people who have this fear or this opposition to the particular proposal now before us are quite justified in this fear. They have plenty of grounds for fearing and for being mistrustful of us who call ourselves white men, because in the past we have had
Indian Act
a fearful record of having broken promises left and right with the Indians. Another reason for this fear and this mistrust or wonderment about losing some of their rights is that initially the right to vote under the law as it is now was connected with the taxation exemption section of the Indian Act. Because this connection was there I am quite sure the Indian people jumped to the conclusion that other rights and privileges were in danger of being taken away as well, and this is the main reason they have some mistrust of and opposition to some parts of this particular bill. Another reason for their opposition is the fear of what might arise out of it, or what they might lose, because they have lost so many things in the past as a result of promises made to them and subsequently broken, not kept or forgotten about.
Another phase-and this is the reason I asked the minister a starred question which was answered yesterday about the number of Indians who had signed taxation waiver exemption forms, when she said the number was 122-is that I think it must be mentioned in the bill before us that the 122 Indians who signed those taxation waiver exemption forms are going to have their taxation waiver forms invalidated by statute so they will no longer be in effect; otherwise we shall have again the two types of Indians when it comes not to voting but to taxation exemption. I hope the minister will look very carefully into this. I think it will require statutory invalidation of the taxation waiver forms that have been signed. The minister shakes her head and says no, it does not require that. I hope she will make a statement now-this may be stretching the rules-without closing the debate.

speechtext: With your permission, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I have a legal ruling on that point from the Department of Justice, and perhaps I might refer to it in order to help the discussion along and so subsequent speakers will not misunderstand. I will read the ruling.

speechtext: Could the hon. lady speak a little louder?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS RIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext:
This is from the Department of Justice. It reads as follows;
... in my opinion, an Indian who has executed such a waiver will enjoy the exemption provided by section 86 (1) of the Indian Act in respect of any liability for tax that would otherwise arise after the day upon which the proposed acts are brought into force by proclamation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS RIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext:
That is very helpful, and eliminates a few comments I was going to make. I am sure these words will be sweet sounding to the 122 people who have signed these taxation waiver forms. If this matter

Indian Act
becomes a question of judicial decision, as might well happen because these things crop up from time to time, I hope the opinion of the justice department just read by the minister will be supported by the court. For argument's sake, if the question of whether or not this is valid should be taken before a court later and the court should rule against the opinion of the justice department, I think it would be extremely unfair to the Indians themselves and we would probably then have to correct the situation. However, that is something for the future.
There is also this point, Mr. Speaker; I am not sure whether the minister mentioned it in her introductory remarks. If she did I missed it, but if she did not I hope when she closes the debate she will indicate to the house that it is the intention to refer the bill to the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Indian affairs that is being established to deal with the Indian Act. As a matter of formality, if for no other reason, I think it would be quite proper to refer the bill to the committee. The committee will have the subject matter before it anyway, and I think that would be the correct thing to do. In addition, the standing committee on privileges and elections is already established, and according to the notice on the order paper the Canada Elections Act is going to be referred to it for study. Perhaps the other bill might be referred to that committee, or they might both go to the same committee inasmuch as they are related.
References were made to section 112 of the Indian Act, which has nothing to do with the right to vote, by the hon. member for Bon-avista-Twillingate and the hon. member for Yukon. It is somewhat beyond the scope of the bill, but perhaps I might be permitted to make one or two brief comments in order that I may disagree with the attitude taken by them. I should like to make my opinion rather clear, because it can be so easily misinterpreted. I said in the committee last year and I say now that I do not think it would be wise to eliminate section 112 entirely. The only part that I think needs to be eliminated is that permitting the compulsory enfranchisement of Indians or a band of Indians whether or not they make application to be enfranchised. In cases where an Indian band may apply for enfranchisement as a band the section does provide for the establishment of a committee of inquiry, and I think it might work out well to leave that part of the section in the act which provides for the appointment of a committee to study and investigate an application for enfranchisement.
I think that would he preferable, rather than eliminating the whole section. I am not entirely persuaded one way or the other with

regard to leaving it in or taking it out, but I do think the compulsory features of the section should be removed entirely so that Indians will not have hanging over their heads the threat of suddenly finding themselves enfranchised, completely divorced from their way of life and forced to accept certain things they did not want in the first place.
In summing up may I reiterate what I think will be some of the beneficial effects arising from the passage of this bill and the one to follow. Not only would it be helpful to the Indian to have a sense of participation in his own affairs, in his own government and parliament; not only will he have the opportunity to become a member of parliament- I hope we will see members of parliament of the Indian race some day-not only will he be exposed to the best democratic ideas and be able to participate fully in the affairs of the nation, but there will be another beneficial effect. If for no other reason than that Indians will become a group of electors, we will see candidates and parties paying more attention to their affairs at the national level. We will see political parties and individual candidates wanting to understand and appreciate the problems of the Indians. We will see parties developing programs and platforms for Indians, and campaigns taking place.
All of this will foe most helpful, because I think members of parties represented in the House of Commons who up to now have not taken too much interest in Indian affairs will, if only for political reasons, come to understand and appreciate the problems of our Indian people and be able to evaluate them more correctly. As a result parliament will have a better understanding of the things that should be done so far as our Indian population is concerned.
Certainly that has been the experience in those provinces where Indians have the right to vote in provincial elections. I know that in my own province of British Columbia, where Indians have had the provincial franchise since 1949, the legislative assembly and the government as entities, not from the party point of view particularly, know more about Indian affairs than any government or legislative assembly prior to 1949. This understanding was assisted to a great degree by the fact that a full blooded Niska Indian from the Nass river region of British Columbia was elected to the legislative assembly, and as one who had lived in that region all his life he was able to give the assembly the benefit of his knowledge and understanding of the problems of the Indians. Because the Indians became a group of

voters, candidates and parties took an interest in them and studied their problems, and the government has a more attentive ear now than was the case before 1949.
I am sure this will be one of the results of Indians being able to participate in federal elections. I do not say that the government and the minister do not have an attentive ear and are not interested. I am not speaking in that sense. I am talking of parties and governments as a whole as they come and go, and of parliament itself. I think members of parliament will have a better understanding and be better able to deal in a fair and decent way with our Indian people, which certainly has not been the case in the past.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS RIGHT TO VOTE IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I take this first opportunity to extend my congratulations to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fair-clough) on her visit last summer to the various Indian bands in western Canada. I know the Indian people of my constituency were most pleased to receive her, and I know that a great many of them had "beefs" which they were quite vocal in presenting to her and her officials. May I say that the minister acquitted herself admirably on this very strenuous trip, and it is certainly looked back upon by the Indians in my territory as a great event.
I should also like to congratulate the minister on bringing in this measure to extend the vote to the Indians without in any way prejudicing their rights and privileges under treaties. May I say that I am not a new adherent to the policy of extending the vote to the Indians. Ten years ago I introduced a similar measure in a model parliament. Little did I think at that time that 10 years later I would have the opportunity of speaking when it was being made the law of Canada.
In some respects it is rather paradoxical that we should be extending this further right of citizenship to those who should be entitled to be called our original and first citizens. It is presumed that the Indians came to North America by migration in prehistoric times from northern Asia by way of the Bering sea. At the time of the first settlement in North America, about four centuries ago, the Indian population of Canada was estimated at about 200,000. Since the advent of the Europeans, however, there has been a steady decline in this population which has given rise to the common phrase, "the vanishing red man". However, in the last half century there has again been an increase, so that today the Indian population of Canada is about 180,000. Of the 180,000 Indians,
Indian Act
slightly less than half will be eligible to vote, so about 80,000 will be eligible. Of these 80,000, about 20,000 already have the privilege of voting. This legislation, therefore, will affect about 60,000 Indians across Canada.
In my own province of Manitoba, there are approximately 24,000 Indians, 3,500 of whom are in my constituency. Of those, about 10,000 or 11,000 will be affected, and about 1,500 in my own riding. In the province of Manitoba the Indians have had the vote since 1952. I believe in the last provincial election their voting record was something like 58 per cent. I believe this is a very favourable percentage when we consider the location of the Indians and how difficult it is for them to get to the polls. I am sure that as time goes by this percentage will steadily increase.
I know there are those in this house who may feel that this step is premature or undesirable. I know there are some Indians who may feel very suspicious of this measure. However, I have written to the chiefs of the seven Indian reservations in my riding. May I say that I did not receive one reply unfavourable to having the vote extended to them. Often in the past these suspicions have been warranted. I know that those Indians who hesitate to welcome this measure extending the vote are doing so because they are afraid that in some manner it may prejudice their rights under the treaties. I believe the Prime Minister and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration have already stated unequivocally that none of these rights will be abrogated when this measure is passed.
In some respects I think the suspicions held by some of these Indians are only natural. I know that in 1945 some of them boycotted family allowances because they had similar suspicions. However, I understand that by 1947 some of those whose suspicions were strongest signed up for family allowances.
As early as 1869 provision was made to grant some measure of local self-government to the Indians. I believe they have had some experience which would assist them in exercising their vote wisely in federal elections. May I point out also that there is no compulsion in this bill. The Indians are to be given a further privilege of citizenship. Whether or not they agree to exercise this privilege is dependent upon themselves. I am sure that those who may at first be reticent about exercising the privilege of voting, as soon as they see we are sincere in extending this measure to them, will exercise their franchise. However, I think this

Indian Act
reticence is overexaggerated, especially in the light of the fine record of the Indians in the provinces where they have the right to vote.
As has been already mentioned by most of the previous speakers, many of the Indians are hesitant about receiving the right to vote while section 112 of the Indian Act remains. I feel in this regard it is only natural that they have tended to confuse the term "enfranchisement", as it is used in the Indian Act, with the term "franchise" as it refers to the vote. Of course this section 112 has never been used, and I believe the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has stated that she does not intend to use it and will not use it. However I feel, like some of the other speakers, that perhaps it would do no harm to the Indian Act to have this section removed. I believe the minister has already committed herself to the removal of the section. In view of this fact I think there is no real basis for the Indians objecting on these grounds.
Under the terms of the agreements and treaties between the Indians and the great white mother, these sovereign people surrendered their independence and pledged their loyalty to the crown. In accepting these treaties the Indians were not often accepted as full citizens. In most cases they became wards of the state rather than citizens exercising all the prerogatives of citizenship and enjoying the rewards resulting from the cession of their lands to the crown.
It is very interesting to note that in 1670, during the reign of Charles II, instructions were given to the effect that Indians desiring to place themselves under British protection should be well received and protected. The British recognized the entitlement of the Indians to the lands in which they roamed. The royal proclamation of 1763 provided that no Indian could be dispossessed of his land without his consent and the consent of the crown, and then only to the crown. In accordance with this principle treaties were made with various Indian tribes during the opening of this country for settlement. Under the terms of those treaties the Indians agreed to cede the land to the crown and pledged their loyalty forever. The Indians in return were granted the reservations and other considerations.
Now, in reality when the Indians signed these treaties they lost their citizenship and their freedom. Since no provision was made for the exercising of the vote by the Indians, and since it was commonly accepted that wards of the state should not be given the privilege of voting, the Indians on reserves

never had this privilege, except in those instances which have already been enumerated.
In accepting these treaties I do not believe the Indians were always cognizant of the limitations contained therein, nor do I believe, in many instances, they were too concerned. They could not readily appreciate the legal phraseology of these treaties. However, what they did understand was the phrase so often used by our Indian chiefs; "the great white mother promised that as long as the sun shone, the rivers flowed and the grass was green, to look after her Indian children like minors". The government of Canada, I feel, has wisely made a determined effort to live up to this faith which the Indians have in us. The government has been consistently extending rights and privileges of citizenship, step by step, to the Indians. The giving of the right to vote to the Indians is just one more in a long line of progressive measures.
In 1951 the Indian Act was amended to permit Indians, at the request of the provinces concerned, to consume intoxicants in public places. Indians have been given this right in British Columbia, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Manitoba, Yukon and Northwest Territories. The Indian Act was again amended in 1956 so that Indians could possess and consume intoxicants on reservations, after a local option vote to do so.

I was trying to show how over a period of time the Indian affairs department has been extending further rights of citizenship. These rights, which we all commonly enjoy and associate with the franchise, have been gradually extended to Indians, and the department has also been assuming a far greater responsibility for the welfare of these Indian citizens than was actually provided for in the act.
Some people argue that the Indians are not yet ready for the vote. My contention has always been that the best way in which to get people to accept responsibility is to give them responsibility. If we look at education alone we will see that whereas in 1948-49, 23,285 Indians were receiving an education, in 1958-59 there was an increase of 15,551 to a total of 38,836. Surely this process of education is preparing the Indians for the wise exercise of their vote.
But most important of all, I think the vote will give the Indians a direct say in the government of their own affairs and in the

manner in which they are governed. They can then vote to change those who govern them if they are not satisfied with the manner in which they are governed and they can use the vote to register a protest against the policies of those who govern them. May I say it also gives them an opportunity to run for office so that they may take a share in this government.
In conclusion may I say that I am most happy that this measure is before the house. I am sure that extending the vote to the Indians will be hailed in the annals of their history as a major step in their emancipation to full citizenship. I hope that one of the ramifications of this bill may be that we shall have one of the Indian people among us as one of our colleagues after the next general election.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on the bill now before this house because there is an Indian reserve in my riding, the Maniwaki reserve, which happens to be located within the limits of the municipality of Maniwaki.
Those Indians are personally known to me, as I have been their dentist for 25 years, and I am perfectly aware of the needs of that tribe.
I must say that the Maniwaki Indians are probably more civilized and cultured than many others in Canada, because they have had the advantage of living among civilized people.
Indian Act
However, we must admit that the white men took advantage of the Indians; they exploited them, as evidenced by what happened at Maniwaki. The town of Maniwaki is part of the Indian reserve of the same name, and, when part of the reserve was detached to form a municipality, the Indians were told to give up those lands and that the proceeds from the sale of those lands would be turned over to the reserve for their benefit.
The Indians had to give up part of their reserve. Well, what happened? A few years later, an appeal was lodged with the privy council which, in its wisdom, rendered a judgment to the effect that Indian reserve lands in Canada did not belong to the reserves proper but to the provinces, so that the Quebec provincial government demanded from the Indian affairs branch in Ottawa a refund of all proceeds from the sale of those lands, and the department did refund the money. The Maniwaki reserve was therefore deprived of part of its territory. Indeed, not only were these Indians dispossessed of a portion of their reserve without getting anything in return, but contractors were allowed to cut part of the best timber in that limit, without any authorization by the majority of the Indian band. Naturally enough, the Maniwaki Indians are somewhat mistrustful today.
Most of the Indians in Maniwaki are educated, some of them highly so, Mr. Speaker. One of them holds a diploma in electronics from the University of Toronto. I do not know of any white man in my riding who is similarly qualified. Some of them are teachers, or nurses, while others occupy various positions in the civil service. They are a highly developed type of Indian. Almost all of them speak three languages: French, English and Algonquin.
Having Indians in our part of the country is a considerable asset. Our district being a tourist area, Indians make excellent guides, for they can speak both English and French, and American tourists, more particularly, are interested in hiring them as guides on hunting or fishing trips. The Indian guide has a special appeal for them because his mentality, his customs and his way of life are different. In addition, he is particularly useful to any tourist who plans to spend several days in the woods. The Indian is also an excellent hunter, and can easily call the bull moose, a distinct advantage in my constituency, a great moose hunting area.
Recently I met a group of Indians of our district, and I must say to the minister and to the house that the Indians of the Maniwaki reserve are opposed to the right to vote.

Indian Act
Quite recently, on television, Mr. Rene Levesque interviewed a group of the most prominent members of the Maniwaki Indian reserve, all of whom stated they were opposed to the right to vote. They are sceptical about it and fear it because they are told it is a privilege being granted to them and one that Maniwaki Indians, at least, do not want.
I think the government would have been well advised, before introducing this bill, to hold a referendum or plebiscite among the Indians, and ask them whether they really want the right to vote.
Today, they are told it is a privilege being granted to them; but nothing guarantees them that in ten, fifteen, twenty or more years from now, voting in Canada will not be compulsory, as it is in some countries, and that Indians will not then be obliged to vote. Today, they don't have to vote, but they have no guarantee that some day the vote will not be compulsory.
Furthermore, we had an experience in the north of Maniwaki, in 1958. For the first time, Indians residing north of Maniwaki, at Forbes Depot, in the constituency of Pontiac-Temis-camingue, were registered on the voters' list and had the right to vote. The group was made up of about sixty families living in hunting territory and not on an organized reserve.
According to the law, those who live in hunting territory have the privilege of voting, like the Indians in the Northwest Territories.
For the first time, in 1958, the names of Indians were included in the voters' list, and they were allowed to vote. The election report of 1957 will bear me out.
In 1957, at Forbes Depot, in the constituency of Temiscamingue 153 voters were on the list. Eighty-four of them voted, 41 in favour of Mr. Martineau and 43 in favour of Mr. Hugh Proudfoot.
In 1958, it was the first time those Indians were voting. That year, Indians were included in the voters' lists and were urged to vote. What was the result? At Forbes Depot, with 337 on the list, only 89 exercised their franchise; 47 voted for Mr. Martineau and 36 for Mr. Hugh Proudfoot, 6 ballots were spoiled. Therefore, there were 5 votes more than in 1957.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like at the outset to congratulate the minister and the government for having brought forward this bill. I think the time is long past due when the Indian people, the original citizens of our country, should be given the right to vote in federal elections in their own country.
There is no question in my mind that the Indians and particularly the ones who live in my constituency will not be able to exercise their franchise properly. They have already demonstrated the fact that they know how to vote and can do so properly. They vote to elect their chiefs and band councils. The members of the band in my constituency

Indian Act
who voted in the last federal election-the ex-servicemen and others who were able to vote-knew how to vote; they voted 100 per cent for this government.
The Indians have a little doubt about the word "enfranchise". They are somewhat prone to confuse the meaning of that word with "enfranchisement", which is a word used in connection with an Indian leaving the band. One of those words in connection with the Indian vote should be changed. I believe the best way to describe the privilege this bill will give them is to say they are being given the right to vote in federal elections.
The Indians at times have difficulty in reconciling the idea of getting something for nothing because previously there has always been some catch to anything they got in a situation comparable to this, at least in the 22 years prior to 1957. The Indians were not at all certain that they were going to be given the vote without any strings attached. However, my people now feel that with this government at the helm they need have no fear about the government going back on its promise or about it introducing amendments to the Indian Act which would abrogate any of their treaty rights of which they are very jealous.
I thought I had a good1 little address all worked out but my friend the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Slogan) happened to have the same thoughts I had and expressed them in his remarks and therefore my speech will be very short. I simply want to reiterate that I am extremely happy to see this bill brought into being which will give the original people of Canada their right to take their place in the economy of their own country. Again I congratulate the minister on bringing forward this legislation and I support it wholeheartedly.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a few words to say about this bill, since there are a few Indian reserves in my constituency.
First of all, I want to say that I will wholeheartedly support this bill because I believe it is the only way to grant Indians a right already enjoyed by all other citizens in Canada. Incidentally, I congratulate the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) for introducing this bill. I believe it provides Indians with a more concrete way of submitting their requests to the authorities of the country.
I have had knowledge of a few instances, where Indians of my constituency have complained about the way they were being treated by certain firms engaged in the fur trading business in various Indian reserves. I

hope this bill will not only encourage Indians to take a more direct interest in their own affairs, but will prompt them to enlist the help of their representatives in this house when seeking to obtain fairer and more equitable treatment.
I have heard of grievances expressed by certain missionaries whose missions are located in my area, and I know that when those grievances were made known to the department, the matter was investigated. I hope that the fact of granting the right to vote to the Indians will prompt them to take an active part in the country's business, as a means of securing for themselves the just and equitable treatment they are entitled to as pioneer citizens of Canada.
Whether we like it or not, Indians are unquestionably Canada's pioneer citizens. If in the past we failed to honour certain commitments-I say if in general we failed to keep our word, I hope that any future agreement will be honoured to the letter.
The previous speaker said that, under this government, the promises that are being made in this bill will be fulfilled. In my view, it would be wise, therefore, to include in this bill all necessary provisions that would guarantee to the Indians the things that they are being promised by this government.
I am happy to support this legislation which will give the Indians of my constituency all the legitimate rights they are entitled to.
