speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when Indian affairs come before this house or before any place in the country to be discussed, immediately they capture the imagination, prompt the reason and stimulate the emotions of the people because there is something about the Indian that fascinates.
I can readily understand the reason why there is a tendency to depart from the question of the matter of the vote which is before the house today. We have often indulged in decrying modern Hitlers and Stalins in annexing other people's land but we never think of our own share in the tragedy of the Indian who dwelt for centuries in the land we now call our own.
Within four centuries we have taken away from the Indians all but a few paltry acres of their vast hunting grounds that stretched from ocean to ocean. The once powerful tribes no longer exist; the descendants, the remnants of the remaining tribes, are hived upon scattered reservations, some 2,226 of them in Canada, eking out an existence and getting sustenance from children of men who were their conquerors.

There will always linger in our memories the tales and legends of the deeds of their warriors and braves on the battlefields, and the eloquence of their chiefs in the long houses, the council houses, as they called them, and yet we cannot help but associate with these memories the sordid tale of cruelty of the strong toward the weak, those who deprived them of the homeland and who still withhold from them the vote of civilization that we prize so highly and prate about.
The Indian from experience has learned that the white man has two tongues, one for the Indian and one for himself. They have been hounded from pillar to post; they have signed peace treaties which have always been broken. They sought peace and never got it until at last they had no place to go. They left the wigwam for the warpath. The time came when all their young men were killed, and consequently they were subdued. With the promises of food, clothing and education for their children, they pitched their tents on the reservations. Today, we have in the bills before us an opportunity to rectify the long standing injustice that we have imposed upon them for so long, the denial to them of the full privilege of the right to an untrammelled vote.
The matter of their equation and transition to a place in our society does not have to be by integration; there can be an accommodation for them as, with their culture and way of life, in spite of all our good intentions, they persist in being what they are. Therefore, let us continue to help them help themselves only with a more abundant substance than heretofore. We are in all conscience obligated to the original natives of our land, to reinstate them in their proper place in our hegemony.
With respect to the bills now before us, it will be recalled that Indians once had the vote in this country. It was given to them by Sir John A. Macdonald back in 1884. After a period of time there was a change in the manhood suffrage in the country, as the minister pointed out in her presentation, and eventually the vote was taken away from them in 1903 by the Laurier regime. Since then they have been in this position. If they were in India they would probably be in the untouchable caste. They have been thought of as wards, but I never regarded them as wards. Down in our hearts we have always wanted to do the right thing by them. All our intentions of doing the right thing by them have been qualified in such a way that they are still in the position of not being equal to the white man.
There is the matter of the treaties that they have entered into. They made treaties 79951-0-122
Indian Act
with the government. Fortunately what we propose to do today is a culmination of all their troubles. Strange as it may seem, some of the Indians do not want the vote. They are fearful because of what happened in the past. They have been promised things but the promises were never realized. They have been deprived of some things that they prize most highly, and their fear is understandable. They still think of all the treaties that were made and broken. They have the idea that we cannot be trusted.
We are going to give them the vote. Let us give it to them unqualified, as we promised to do. I do not think we should say in the bill that the giving of the vote is not going to interfere with anything they enjoy today. If we tell them this they will think we are trying to palm something off on them. You know what happens when you are offered something and you are told that it contains everything that you want. You are a little suspicious that there is something underhand about it because the person is so emphatic in insisting that there is nothing wrong with it. The Indian cannot be blamed if he takes the same attitude. Therefore, when we give the Indian the vote let us give it to him without any qualifications. Do not let us arouse his suspicion by saying that it does not take any of his rights away. If there is any question about what the legislation means it will be properly interpreted in due course by the courts, and I have enough confidence in the courts to believe that they will read in it just exactly what it says, and that the Indian will get his rights.
Mention was made of the standing of the Indians in regard to the population of the country. I have been checking over the figures from the department and I see that Ontario still stands out with a population of close to 42,000. British Columbia has the largest number of reservations and bands, with Ontario next, and so on down the line. Even if all the Indians were given the vote they could not make a great impact on the country, and I do not understand why people should fear that they are going to upset anything. Let them take their natural place in the community, the same as the rest of us. For some reason or other there seems to be a fear that they cannot look after themselves. They are no different from any others. There are the good and there are the bad, the same as any other segment of our population.
The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) mentioned treaty rights in this country, and also the treaty with the Indians in Ontario, particularly the Six Nations. The difficulty with them is that they have a different set-up.

Indian Act
They claim that they have treaties with two countries through alliances with Britain and France and that they were allied with the British and the French in bygone years. The alliances and treaties that were made were honoured by those kings and were also recognized at the time of the conquest and the capitulation at Montreal. The Indians' rights were continued and the validity of their treaties accepted.
The treaties of the government with other Indian bands are in a different category. The Six Nations Indians claim they were an ally and therefore they have a different status from other Indians. They say that they have an unwritten agreement and in support of that they meet once a year at Niagara Falls and have a ceremony or celebration in which they walk across the border and back without let or hindrance. They can purchase what they want without any duty being levied.
There is an international relationship involved in the case of the Six Nations Indians. They are on both sides of the border. When the battle of independence took place and the Indians had to make a choice some of them chose Canada and most of them are on the Six Nations reserve at Brantford. There is a difference between their treaty and the treaties that other Indians bands in the country have. The rebellious element in the Six Nations Indians mostly live south of the border and they insist upon their status as a nation. They claim they are a separate entity and are not citizens of Canada. The Indian affairs branch has always been co-operative and have amicable relations with the Six Nations Indians who live in Canada.
The giving of the vote to the Indians on the Six Nations reserve is only giving back to them what they had from Sir John A. Macdonald. I believe if we pass this legislation and give them the vote it will go a long way toward securing for them the status which righfully belongs to them. We should set them up as a respected people who have had a vested interest in this land long before we did and accord them the dignity and prestige they deserve so that they may again have a culture of their own. Their way of life can fit into ours and we should not make them be something that they do not want to be.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as chairman of the Indian affairs committee during the last session, I was able to learn a lot about Indians, and this knowledge was all the more valuable to me because in my

riding, unfortunately, there are no more survivors of the Indian people who in the past were the only citizens of this country.
The legislation now under consideration seems to me to be democratic to a high degree and I must admit that none of the objections expressed so far have either impressed or convinced me. First of all, the purpose of this legislation is to give the Indian the right to vote without any restriction. It opens the door so to speak to Canadian democracy for 175,000 people scattered throughout the country. It will allow those people to take part in the affairs of our country and will foster in them a sense of democracy.
In view of the purpose of this legislation, I think we must support it beyond all question.
I listened earlier to certain objections or certain restrictions made by the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc). He mentioned some specific cases. I am not in a position to disprove his arguments nor to agree with him. What I saw with my own eyes is very different. In the county of Quebec, where I live, there is a Huron reservation and I must recognize that the Indians of that reservation often set an example for us white men. I have never thought and don't now believe that general conclusions can fairly be drawn from scenes such as those described by the hon. member for Gatineau. That would be altogether inconsistent.
My good colleague mentioned the possibility of a referendum. Of course, that would be a way to go about it. Still, if Indians in his riding who were entitled to vote did not even take advantage of this right in certain circumstances, for reasons that I know nothing about, how could we find out about the wishes of the same Indians through a referendum? This suggestion seems inconsistent to me and could not be considered.
As a matter of fact, I believe that responsibility for such legislation rests with parliament and that it is up to hon. members of this house to assume that responsibility.
The Indian problem is one of the problems of concern to hon. members, to parliament, and to the government. We have, with regard to that Indian problem, a legislation which has been progressively improved, a legislation which might, before long, call for other amendments or other improvements. The matter we are now considering, should be settled by the members of parliament, without subterfuge or evasion or any attempts to shift responsibility upon anyone else.
That is why I believe this bill must come to a vote. As I said the bill implies no restric-

tions. It widens the scope of activities of the Indians, and enables them, in a most direct and democratic way to have a say in their own affairs in so far as they are under the jurisdiction of the federal government.
I do not know a single basic objection that might be raised against this legislation.
Moreover, it is bound to give the Indian a greater feeling of pride. It will rid his mind of that sort of inferiority complex that is likely to develop in a group which sometimes feels that it is living under trusteeship in comparison to other groups of fellow citizens who enjoy full democratic rights.
I believe that by exercising this right, the Indian will feel closer to other Canadians and that there will be more fraternization between them. This legislation will mean a further step toward the Canadian unity we are all striving for.
Mr. Speaker, much has been said, and rightly so-the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc) mentioned it, and I perfectly agree with him on this point-of the degree of culture which several Indian nations have reached.
I must say that as co-chairman of the Indian affairs committee last year, I was singularly impressed and even amazed by the degree of culture of the representatives who appeared before us to state their grievances and make the recommendations they wanted carried out through our Indian affairs legislation.
As to the standard of the briefs submitted to us, they were really remarkable and proved the very high degree of civilization attained by those Indian nations. They definitely feel that Indians and Canadians are brothers, that such a brotherhood is a kind of protection for their faith, culture and development, and I cannot see that in granting them the right to vote which opens to them, so to speak, the door of democracy, we are likely to create suspicion against us, especially when this right to vote, I repeat, involves no restriction of any kind and does not infringe in any way upon the legislation under which they are now living and upon the rights and liberties which it officially recognizes.
Mr. Speaker, I am not unaware of my incompetence in this matter, and that is why you will allow me, in closing, to voice an argument that carries the weight of authority. They are the words spoken on July 2, or 3 last, before our joint committee on Indian 79951-0-122J
Indian Act
affairs, by Reverend Kelly, chairman of the legislative committee of the native brotherhood of British Columbia.
From that issue of the report, I shall quote in particular from page 138. I believe the conclusions put forward by Reverend Kelly should be such as to put an end to any discussion on that problem and to inspire us to confidence in voting the measure introduced by the minister of immigration.
The Indians of British Columbia feel very strongly that they should have the federal vote on the same basis on which the provincial vote was granted them. Before this vote was granted to them, there was a fear in the minds of a good many of them that somehow the exercising of that franchise would jeopardize their status as Indians. By experience, they have learned that it has enhanced their position in the province, and they are now grateful for the day when this was made possible for them.
On the same basis, there are many Indians throughout the country who have raised their voices against the federal vote. They think that the extension of the federal vote would weaken their position in retaining their aboriginal rights and possessions. But careful consideration of the whole situation makes the executive committee of the native brotherhood of British Columbia, as well as the whole rank and file of the membership, feel that the British Columbia vote gave them a new appreciation of their position in the province, and that the federal vote would be equally beneficial.
In other words, Reverend Kelly stresses the educational value, a democratic educational value, involved in the exercise of franchise by British Columbia Indians, and that educational value is precisely the one which, today, causes those same Indians to wish to share in the benefits to which we are entitled through franchise. A little farther on Reverend Kelly said:
The provincial vote has been granted to Indians in the provinces of British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. As we have pointed out, it has in no way interfered with their aboriginal or treaty rights, and we believe the federal vote will give them a greater sense of pride and responsibility in their place as citizens of Canada.
Since many of the members of the government now in power supported this position of granting the federal vote to the Canadian Indians, we are glad to bring this matter up and press for its fulfilment at this time. We are confident that the present Prime Minister, the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, would be glad to have the opportunity of initiating the fulfilment of this long-delayed right of citizenship.
As we represent the British Columbia Indians, we can only speak for the native people of that province. We would like to say that we would appreciate if the federal vote were granted to our people on the same basis on which the British Columbia provincial vote was granted to them.

Indian Act
In other words, Mr. Speaker, you have there the expressed opinion of a prominent Indian who fulfils a very important function among his fellow Indians and who also speaks with a wisdom based on the soundest principles of philosophy and who emphasizes how valuable an experience it was for those Indians of British Columbia and probably for those of the other provinces to exercise their right to vote.
Therefore, I believe that that argument is stronger than all the others and disposes of the few objections against this bill. I read with interest, in particular the speech of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), and I do not know-naturally this is a personal opinion-I do not know of any legal contradiction between this bill, as introduced, and the guarantees contained in the Indian Act. I do not find in this bill any restriction to the existing legislation and the slightest infringement upon the rights already belonging to the Indians of the country.
For those reasons I support this measure. (Text):

I am sure the Indians living in the constituency I represent will receive very warmly the legislation that is before the house at the present time. I have two reservations in my area, both occupied by the Sioux Indians, and for the past few years they have taken an increasing interest in public affairs. In the first instance, this interest arose as a result of the right to vote in provincial elections. I have worked very closely with them in public matters, and it was always a very difficult problem to explain to them when federal elections came along why they did not have the opportunity to vote on federal issues. I have, therefore, no hesitancy at all in giving wholehearted support to the measure that is before us.
We have had a rather extended discussion on this matter and I do not intend, at this stage in our discussion, to rehash the trials and tribulations of our first Canadians. Suffice it to say that the time is long past due when we should take steps such as the step which is contemplated by this legislation to bring our Indian population into the stream of Canadian life.
This granting of the right to vote, of course, is not to be interpreted as a panacea. It is merely one short step in the direction of breaking down the isolation, the segregation and the paternalism of the reserve system and helping our first Canadians become integrated into the Canadian way of life for the first time. It seems to be a remarkable thing to me that it has taken so long for the white
tMr. Dorion.l
population, the majority population of this country, to come to grips with this problem of restoring our first Canadians to the rights of full citizenship. In this whole process I think that the right to vote is a helpful and positive contribution and will encourage not only the Indian population to exercise their rights as citizens but also the majority group of the Canadian population to take a closer, more intimate interest in the problems of our first Canadians.
Just in passing, Mr. Speaker, may I say that if this right to vote is going to mean anything in terms of helping the Indian in the direction toward complete citizenship, we will have to think in terms of the educational process involved.
We all know that one of the difficulties of bringing the newly independent nations into the democratic scheme of things is the educational problem involved in encouraging an appreciation of not only the mechanics of voting, the mechanics of exercising the right to vote, but also of the ideas and the values which lie behind cur democratic system.
Recently the department of Indian affairs has been making some encouraging advances in the field of education. If there were time in which to do so, I could quote statistics in this regard. However, I should like to suggest that if the right to vote is to be exercised in an intelligent way by our Indian population across the nation we shall be obliged to move into the adult education field on the reserves. We now have located on reservations schools which provide the facilities to begin what is known as a lighted school movement amongst the population on the reserves. By that I mean that not only can the children be helped in the educational process but the members of the older generation, the parents of the children, can be brought together in the evening through the facilities provided by reservation schools and can be helped in understanding what is involved in the right to vote and the responsibilities of Canadian citizenship.
This leads me to one final thought. If we are going to resolve the problems that the years of isolation and segregation have caused in the Indian population, the communities surrounding these reservations must become actively interested in the Indian population. The right to vote is going to be welcomed by a vast majority of our first Canadians but unless there is an equally positive response from the larger communities I am afraid it is not going to help too much in the forward movement. Prejudice will have to go as well as the insensitivity that prevails to a large extent on the part of the majority of the population towards this minority group.

For example, I could mention the stereotypes indicating the attitude the majority has towards the Indians. They are to the effect that he is slothful, he is lazy, he is immoral and so on and so forth. The fact of the matter is, of course, that our Indian population had a way of life that we destroyed and we took no steps to replace his nomadic tribal way of life by bringing him into close relationship with the white man's civilization. Discrimination, both physical and psychological, must end before our first Canadians will regain the feeling of human dignity and before they will enjoy their rightful heritage of once again feeling at home in their own country. This is, of course, a job for voluntary organizations on all levels of our Canadian life: on the national level, on the provincial level and on the local level. Church groups have a particular responsibility in this regard.
In passing legislation of this kind the government of Canada provides the means for bringing the Indian population out from behind what we might call the buckskin curtain, or the shadow of segregation in which they have lived for so long. But it is the voluntary groups, the communities in which these Indians live, which must provide the necessary point of human contact to give our first Canadians the sense of belonging.

In the first place may I say that I endorse it wholeheartedly. The reason why I feel I should say a few words in the debate is that there are two large reservations in the constituency of Bow River, comprising first the Blackfoot reserve near Gleichen, Alberta and, second, the Morley Sarcee reserve. The ancestors of these Indians roamed the prairies of Saskatchewan and Alberta in those days when the buffalo roamed the prairies and was their sole source of food. When the early settlers came from 1875 to 1885, during the time when the Canadian Pacific railway was pushing westward to bring together this great country which today comprises the ten provinces, large herds of buffalo roamed the prairies. That was the source of food for the Indian.
The import of the few remarks I have to make is that when the settlers came in, the buffalo herds disappeared. Then, of course, it was as a result of that situation that the white man was obliged to set up some type of reservation. It was this reserve to which
Indian Act
the Indian went, and by virtue of the treaties that set up the reserves and the Indian Act his rights exist today.
I feel the main reason why a person should voice his opinion and support this legislation is that over the years since the time the reservations were set up the Indian has, either directly or indirectly, received what I might call the castor oil treatment. He was told, "This is what is good for you; open your mouth; here it is." For the first time we have this type of legislation giving the Indian the right to express himself as to what type of schools he will have, what kind of hospitals he will have, how he will make his living and provide the food to replace the buffalo herds, what kind of law and order should exist in the reservation itself, what type of sociability he will have and what kind of political life he will have, and even to express himself in his own spiritual way as to what kind of religion he will have.
It is because of this fact that I endorse the legislation and congratulate the minister for presenting it yesterday. I might say I thought it was an excellent thing last year when the minister-for the first time that one reserve had had a minister visit there in 23 years-came to the reservation itself, sat down at noon and dined with the Indian chiefs, their councillors and the Indians themselves and heard the Indians express their ideas. After all, we cannot boast of our system of democracy in this country with impunity as long as we have citizens who do not enjoy the right to vote.
While the minister has given every assurance that none of the ancient rights of the Indians will be usurped or abrogated, there is still in the minds of many Indians, on the reservations especially, an inherent suspicion of the words "franchise" and "enfranchisement". When the term "the right to vote" is used there is no way in which there can be any misinterpretation of the meaning of this bill. Consequently, it should meet with the approval of the majority of those concerned.
Naturally, I do not want to anticipate what response this action will have in the minds of the Indians. We must realize that our responsibility does not end with the granting of the vote and that this action may, in effect, be the basis for further legislation. However, with this legislation there should be a tendency toward a greater feeling of equality and, naturally, integration.
The approach to this matter should be facilitated if we bear in mind that our Indians, both in history and in legend, have been recognized as a proud and independent
Indian Act
people, and that extending the voting privilege is one way of re-establishing the dignity of the Indian not only in his mind but in the minds of other citizens as well. It may well be that in the granting of the right to vote we may encourage a return to those characteristics for which Indians were respected and admired. Should this be the case, we must also be prepared to expect demands for further adjustments in the Indian way of life.
Having been given the vote the Indians will naturally want a freedom of choice in other matters as well. While the indiscriminate granting of some of the requests could not be considered without contravening the terms of the Indian Act, it is reasonable to suppose that after acquiring the vote the Indian may want to be in a position to purchase land of his own, to dispose of his products without the interference of the Indian agent and to have his children integrated in the provincial school systems. Subsection (1) does not apply to or in respect of the personal property of an Indian who has executed a waiver under the provisions of paragraph (e) of subsection (2) of section 14 of the Canada Elections Act.
On this section the intention seems to be that the Indian will have a complete right to vote; but what I am concerned with is this. The hon. lady said yesterday that 122 Indians have signed such a waiver. According to my own judgment-I might be wrong -it might be that those who have signed the waiver will, after the bill is passed and becomes law, be under the liability, I might say, of that waiver or will still suffer from it.
I now read section 19 of chapter 158 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, which is the Interpretation Act and if I may I will read only the pertinent section. Subsection (1) reads as follows:
Where any act or enactment is repealed, or where any regulation is revoked, then, unless the contrary intention appears, such repeal or revocation does not, save as in this section otherwise provided-
And then there follow paragraphs (a), (b) and (c). Paragraph (c) seems to me to be the relevant paragraph. I will go back:
-such repeal or revocation does not, save as in this section otherwise provided,
(c) affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired1, accrued, accruing or incurred under the act, enactment or regulation so repealed or revoked.

As I said, the repeal does not affect any obligation or liability acquired, accrued, accruing or incurred under the act. I may be wrong, and the minister in her reply will probably give us some light on that and will cite the opinion of the Department of Justice, but in my own mind the Indians who signed the waiver did incur an obligation or liability because they became subject to taxation. The repeal of the act, as the Interpretation Act states, does not affect that obligation. Therefore, I would think, although I endorse the bill completely because I am in favour of every Canadian having the right to vote, there should be provision in the bill protecting the rights and treaties and also making it clear that those 122 Indians will not in the future be affected by the waiver they have signed.

I should like to make this other observation to the hon. lady. What conceivable harm could it do, in order to make sure that this liability which these people incurred, in order that these 122 people may be able to vote, to put an express provision in this bill to say that the liability will no longer exist when this bill becomes law? Whether or not it is an implication of the repeal that that would be the case, an express provision to that effect would remove all shadow of doubt. I do not want to labour this point.
My hon. friend from Gatineau, who has a number of constituents who are Indians and who have the vote and a number of others who are Indians and who have not the vote, has told us this afternoon that the Indians in his riding do not want the vote. They are 79951-0-123J

suspicious of it. We do know that suspicion exists in the minds of many Indians in many parts of the country. I think, sir, as I said on second reading, everything we can do to remove that suspicion amongst all the Indians, not just the majority of them-I am sure the majority of them do want the vote, of course-should be done. There seems to be no argument on the other side of the matter at all.
Nothing would be more unfair, nothing would be more contrary to anyone's conception of natural justice than to leave these 122 people, who were sufficiently patriotic, sufficiently democratic, sufficiently interested in the exercise of the vote to give up a right which all the other Indians continue to have, for one single day under even a shadow of any disability. I would urge the hon. lady, between now and eight o'clock to consider whether it would not be better to remove this beyond the shadow of a doubt by putting another provision in the bill which would remove this liability.
Frankly, I was very disappointed that the hon. lady should have said what she did about my suggestion with regard to putting an express provision in the bill, either by way of preamble or, as I think is preferable, by way of a declaratory provision. As the hon. lady knows, in the citizenship act the first provision is a declaratory provision. As I reminded the hon. lady when she was speaking a few minutes ago, the Prime Minister is proposing later in this session to introduce a bill to set out the rights of the rest of us. It does seem to me that a declaratory provision put into this bill, saying that the exercise of the vote under the Canada Elections Act, or some language to that effect, would not in any way jeopardize any rights, whether by treaty, by custom or by statute now enjoyed or prior to the enactment of the section we are now proposing in the bill were enjoyed by Indians, would solve the problem. It is one thing for those of us who sit in parliament to state that that is the law. However, I know that the hon. lady would not expect me to be as much impressed by her assurance or the Prime Minister's assurance or even by my assurance, that no one would ever do anything about this. If we could put it in the law, then let us put it in the law. Then, it will not be a matter of somebody's assurance.
I recall, of course, when the leader of the government was sitting over here he used to be very fond of talking, as did the present Minister of Justice, about government by laws and not by men. I admit that the hon. lady is completely right when she contends that this legislation, as it is, will take away no rights whatever. Of course she is right.

I accept that, and I am sure everyone in this house accepts it. There is no question about that. However, we have heard debates in this house at other times about the use of the French language. We have heard debates concerning other cherished rights of minorities in this country. None of those minorities want these rights to be based upon assurance; each of them wants those rights to be based upon the law. Here we are legislating in respect of people who do not yet have a vote, and who have no share in the procedure of electing us. We are making a law apply to them.
We know that many of them are suspicious of what we are doing. We think they are wrongly suspicious, in fact, we are confident they are wrongly suspicious. However, that does not alter the fact they are suspicious. I do think if we do everything we can properly do to remove that suspicion, we would be wise. I do hope that the hon. lady will between now and eight o'clock take one more look at this suggestion.

This resume has been related to me by someone else. If I have stated incorrectly what the minister has said, I hope she will correct me.
But if that is the general gist of what was said-and the minister nods her head so I take it that it has been correctly related-I would point out that it is still my opinion, now that we are in committee, that this committee should not be dealing at this moment with this particular bill but that it should have gone to the Indian affairs committee. After all, that was the purpose, or one of the purposes, of passing that motion yesterday to establish a joint committee. The terms of reference of that committee include the Indian Act. This is a part of it. In the committee proceedings of last year reference was made by delegations which appeared before the committee to the specific question before us now.
I have had the opportunity to have a preview look at some of the briefs which have been prepared for presentation to the committee this year and I may say there is a good bit of reference in those briefs to this self-same subject matter of the right to vote. I still think the bill should have gone to that particular committee for discussion and that it should not at this moment be being dealt with in a committee of the whole house. I do not think what I said is one bit inconsistent with what I had to say in other sessions or indicates a desire to delay the passage of the bill. Last year, as the minister may recall-and certainly a look at Hansard will bear it out-when I had the honour of introducing a similar bill I at that time suggested that the house should either refer the bill or the subject matter to the Indian affairs committee. In the session prior to that one I dealt with the same question.
I do not recall whether the discussion was on the bill to amend the elections act or the Indian Act, but it was on the same subject matter, and the recommendation I made then was that it should have been referred two sessions ago to the committee on privileges and elections for the purpose of allowing interested people to express their views. This opportunity is, of course, not afforded in the committee of the whole. I still think that that would be the proper course to take.
The suggestion which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has made regarding some of the provisions which might properly be included in this bill is, I submit, another reason for sending this piece of legislation to the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Indian affairs. We all know how difficult it is to amend legislation,

Indian Act
even when the government desires to amend its own legislation, in committee of the whole where there are potentially some 260 points of view which could be expressed. How much easier it would be to draft legislation of this kind if the bill had been referred to the joint committee where interested parties could express their ideas about the principle involved and where we could also have the benefit of some legal opinion as to whether or not the waiver forms would be invalidated by this legislation if it were passed.
It is possible that the form of amendment now proposed is not appropriate. The wording of such amendments is, as I am sure the minister will agree, best done by legal officials within government circles who have had a great deal of experience in this field. I am not saying that the proposed amendment is incorrect, but we all find in presenting amendments that they could perhaps be more correctly drafted by those people who have spent a great deal of time doing this work. In the committee we would have more opportunity to consider the point of view expressed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
I am sure it is the wish of everyone in this house that the people who have signed these forms should not, under the legislation now to be disposed of, be placed in a position different from that of any other Indian. That is the desire of us all. This being so, I think we should say so specifically in the legislation, making it clear that this waiver form is not valid any longer. We should spell that out in the act. As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate pointed out, once this act passes into law there will be no reference in the statutes for Canada to any taxation waiver forms to say what they mean or what they do not mean.
A second point is this. A very large number of Indian people feel they have been unjustly treated by the so-called white men and by governments in particular. They were promised or guaranteed certain rights and privileges, and as time went on they discovered that these promised rights and privileges were withheld. For a number of years Indians were of the opinion that the so-called Jay treaty applied to them and enabled them to cross the border between Canada and the United States and to carry all the goods they liked with them, without being subject to duty. This is not strictly within the terms of the bill, Mr. Chairman, but I think it is relevant to the subject under discussion. It was not until this question was referred to the Supreme Court of Canada that it was ruled that the Jay treaty did not, in fact, apply to the Indians, because it had not been

given statutory authorization by the parliament of Canada. This is one case of the Indians having been promised that certain things would exist to their advantage, and then finding subsequently that they were not entitled to the expected benefit.
I do not wish to say positively that something similar will occur as far as these 122 Indians who signed waiver forms are concerned. However, I think it would be disastrous if parliament, having indicated that it wants to ensure that these forms should not have any validity, were to bring about a similar result by failing to make its intentions clear. I am sure this is the attitude taken by the hon. minister. It is the attitude of the Department of Justice. It is, I know, the attitude of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, and it is our attitude also.
This is an actual commitment which we are making. It will be on record in Hansard for years to come, to the effect that the Indian people will all be in the same class, that is to say, not to be taxed in respect of personal property on the reserve even though a waiver form might have been signed some years ago. This is our intention, and if in years to come the question is taken to court concerning the validity of these waiver forms, once this bill has become law, it would be extremely unfair to the Indian people if they were suddenly to discover that the opinion expressed by the minister and obtained from the Department of Justice was held to be invalid by a decision of the courts.
What we are offering to the Indians amounts to a commitment, and if what I have suggested did occur it will be another of the white man's broken promises, and a further failure on our part to take advantage of another opportunity to show that we mean what we say. I would much prefer to see this commitment included in statutory form in order to ensure that the 122 people who have signed waiver forms will not be taxed. I would like to see this undertaking given statutory validity and so, I am sure, would the minister herself. I do not think we should take any kind of gamble with regard to a commitment made to the Indian people. I think the minister should indicate that she believes the suggestion made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to be a sound one, and should agree to put it into the form of a statutory declaration. It may be that the words used by the hon. member are not the best possible words, but I do not believe the hon. member is insisting on the exact wording which he has put forward. It is better to make this declaration now in statutory form rather than find in years to come that we had a chance to guarantee it but failed to take the opportunity to do so.

With due respect to my friend from Hull, I think he is quite a bit out of date in this particular case. This is not imposing anything on anyone. It would be an imposition if the ideas suggested by some members of the Liberal party were put into effect and the voting were made compulsory; then it would be an imposition upon the Indians to be forced to register and to be forced to vote. This is not an imposition. It has been an imposition for so many years to deny them the right to vote, but certainly it is not an imposition to grant to the Indians of this country freedoms that have been enjoyed by so many people in this and other countries, that is the right to have the franchise and select members of parliament.
If the Indian does not want to have his name registered as a voter, he does not have to do so. He is in the same position as anyone else. If the Indian does not want to vote on election day, that is his business and he does not have to do so. The same situation exists now in the provinces of Ontario, British Columbia, Manitoba and Nova Scotia with respect to provincial elections. The Indians in those provinces have the vote. Some of them exercise it and some of them do not, just the same as non-Indians do. There is absolutely no imposition in this. It has been an imposition for too many years now and we are attempting to remove the imposition.

Mr. Chairman, I must take issue with my hon. friend from Hull because the Indians, and those interested in their welfare, were certainly heard in the committee meetings which were held in the years 1946, 1947 and 1948. After this committee had met and made its report it was found that one of the recommendations which emanated from the deliberations of that committee was that the vote should be given to the Indians. In the intervening time many groups of Indians have made representations, by briefs and by personal appearances, to the department. We have a record of the representations which have been made and the organizations from which those representations have come. We have a record in the department of representations in favour of the Indians having the right to vote, without restriction, from eleven different organizations. We have representations expressing opposition from seven organizations, but the eleven who are in favour represent a voting population of a minimum of 30,000 and the seven who are opposed represent a voting population of not more than 4,000. You have, therefore, 30 to 4 or 7J to 1 votes in favour of the Indian's right to vote.
I should like to point out what has been stated earlier in the course of this debate, and that is that this is not compulsory voting. The Indians may vote or may not vote as they wish, just as the non-Indian populace does. It is a pretty good vote in a federal election that turns out 70 per cent of the voters. In the various provinces in which the Indians have the vote provincially they have turned out a very good percentage, having consideration for the fact it is a new venture for them and that they have not been educated to it,

as well as the fact that in various parts of the country they are opposed to voting, as my hon. friend has said. If the Indians in the province of Quebec do not wish to vote, that is their privilege. If the Indians in the rest of Canada do wish to vote I hope it will now be their privilege to vote.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE INDIANS THE RIGHT TO VOTE
speechtext:
Since we have heard a few remarks from the hon. member for Hull who seems to be the self-appointed defender of the Indians in Quebec, I should like to add a few remarks. I think I have more Indians in my riding than he has in his. I can tell him that most of them have been voting for many years because they do not live on the reservation. I think we can generally say that the Indians will vote on the reserve. The Indians who live on the reserve do not want the vote right now. Those who do not live on the reserve have been voting for years. They are for this measure. I am sure over the years all the Indians will approve this measure and will vote freely in every election.
In the riding of Chapleau which I represent the Indians vote federally and provincially only those living on the reserve, and there are very few living on the reserve. They have been given the right to vote and they have exercised that right; and to the surprise possibly of my friend the hon. member for Hull-and he can check the record-they have been voting Liberal in many cases except in the last election because, I suppose, of policy by this government. I am sure if he checks the record he will see that many of the Indians at Rupert House, Eastmain, Nemiscau, Mistassini and Waswanipi have voted in every federal election except in 1957 when their names could not be put on the list in time for that election. I do not know what the Liberals did at that time. They did not make the list in time. In the election which took place in June, 1958 they had the right to vote and many of them voted Liberal and Conservative as well.

Whereas the Indian Act provides for the provincial vote for Indians, and
Whereas the Indians in three provinces and the Northwest Territories have already accepted the provincial vote when it was offered to them by the provincial government, and
Whereas the removal of section 112 from the act would make it impossible for an Indian to become enfranchised against his will for any reason, such as taking the vote,

Resolved that the Indian association of Alberta goes on record as approving the principle of Indians accepting the provincial or the federal vote without any loss of treaty rights.

I have the greatest possible respect for the views of the hon. member for Hull but I feel we are taking the right course in giving the Indians the right to vote if they want to vote. That is all we shall be doing by passing these two bills. However, I think it will be a very sad and unfortunate thing-and something the government itself and the hon. lady in particular will regret-if this act giving all Indians the vote is not marked in some way on the statutes. All we are doing is to repeal, as we are doing, a section in one act and a section in another act and there is no record anywhere of the fact that something positive has been done. I am going to make a suggestion, and the hon. lady can change this around in any way she likes. I will send a copy over to her right away so that she can read it while I am reading it. I would suggest that the hon. lady ask for unanimous consent to put into this bill a short preamble setting out its purpose so that there will be on the records of parliament and permanently in the statute books a record of what we are now doing. The way in which I have drafted it-and I am not wedded to the particular wording-is this:
Whereas it is expedient that the Indians of Canada should have the right to vote under the Canada Elections Act without jeopardy to any rights or privileges whether by treaty custom or statute now enjoyed by them and that the rights waived by certain Indians to qualify for the vote under the existing law should be restored.
Then it would go on from there "Her Majesty" and so on. I think it speaks for itself.

I recognize the good intentions of my hon. friend and I am sure we all feel the same way about these two pieces of legislation; but any such addition to either bill would be merely gilding the lily. However, this particular preamble suggested by my hon. friend in my opinion covers a great deal of territory without regard to what the implications might be. The main thing that bothers all of us-and has bothered us-is those 122 waivers that are outstanding. As I have said before, I am assured that those waivers will be null and void after these bills receive royal assent. For that reason I really cannot see any great virtue in it.

As with the last bill that was passed, I think we should keep in mind first the people who are to be affected by the bill. Primarily, it is the Indian people themselves. Others are affected in an incidental way and as time goes on they will be more greatly affected by the impact of the exercise of the vote by various Indian people across the country. But keeping in mind the people who will be affected immediately-and that is the Indian people themselves-and knowing that they have fears, that they wonder whether the right to vote is connected with any possible loss of treaty rights-of course we know that it is not-or any possible loss of their hereditary or aboriginal rights which they have had over the years and which have been recognized in law and in various statutes at different times. I think that putting in some few words similar to those suggested or with this intent would be extremely beneficial to the Indians themselves and once more would be a statutory declaration of this parliament that we are making with the Indian people a bargain that we do not intend to break. If we put it in statutory form to show to them as a further indication of our honesty, our sincerity and our desire not to have these commitments broken at some later date-and I do not think they are going to be broken- as a mark in the statute, if nothing more than a commemoration, as suggested by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I personally think it would be a fair, decent and sincere thing to have expressed in this particular statute at this time.

It is a well established rule, I think, that when an act or part of an act is to be repealed, it cannot be done merely by implication. It has to be clearly stated. I can recall, although somewhat vaguely, the rule set by Maxwell in Interpretation Statutes. I am pretty sure that repeal by implication cannot exist without very serious reasons. I do not find anything in this bill which could be interpreted against the rights and liberties of Indians, as already set forth in the existing Indian Act.
If we had been given a concrete example to work on, and which would enable us to say: This is a situation that could occur; how could it be reconciled with this bill, and how could it be corrected unless the preamble of the present act does include the statement of principle which we are suggesting? Then, in that case, I would have been prepared to accept the hon. member's suggestion. But I fail to see how such a situation could arise. Moreover, I repeat, I fail to see by what implication resulting from this bill one could come to the conclusion that any right or liberty guaranteed by the existing Indian Act could be repealed. That is why I am ready to support the bill in its present form.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my remarks at this time will be rather brief. However, I should like to express my wholehearted support of the amendment to the National Housing Act to provide more money for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans. This measure, I am sure, will be most welcomed by the construction industry in general all across Canada and I am sure it will also be welcomed by a great many people who are contemplating becoming home owners. There may be some areas in Canada where the supply of housing is catching up with the demand but there still exists in most parts of Canada today a considerable shortage of housing.
In rising to take a small part in this debate I do so with some background in the construction industry and I should like, as I go along, to make some suggestions to the minister which he might take into consideration.
First of all I wish to stress the importance of good housing for the health and welfare of our people and the need to provide healthful and pleasant surroundings in which to raise our children. Housing for Canadians is a broad subject. One could say much about the high cost of new homes today and tax burdens home owners have to carry and touch upon a number of other problems that are contributing to the high cost of


home ownership and home rental. These conditions are reaching the danger point at which even people in the medium wage brackets find it difficult to provide homes for themselves either by building or by renting without municipal or governmental subsidies.
Since this debate is relative to supplying mortgage funds for home building under the existing C.M.H.C. regulations I will confine my remarks to matters pertaining to the subject which is before us at the present time.
First of all may I say to the Minister of Public Works that his action in introducing an amendment to supply mortgage money to the house building industry is highly commendable and this assistance will be welcomed. It will result in far-reaching effects and will serve to provide employment for many thousands of Canadians.
The construction industry is the most important factor in Canada's national economy. No other industry can provide such a variety of jobs in such a short time as house building. The products of our forest, of our sand and stone quarries, of our lime, cement and brick factories, as well as other natural resources, are required immediately at the start of the construction of a house. This is followed by other products such as plumbing supplies, heating furnaces, oil and gas burners, and so on down the line, until the construction job is finished, when the merchants in most cases move in with the drapes, rugs, furniture and the cooking appliances, to make a complete job.
An average six-room bungalow costing between $12,000 and $14,000 employs on the job-that is, on the construction job-an average of eight labourers for two weeks, 16 weeks in all; two bricklayers for four weeks, eight weeks in all; four carpenters, four weeks, 16 weeks in all; two plumbers, one a week, two weeks in all; one metal worker; one electrician; two painters, two weeks, four weeks in all; two plasterers one week; one tile setter, one week; or a visible payroll of approximately $4,000 per house and approximately 2,000 manhours of labour not including the component parts that go into the house in the form of manufactured goods and other products I have already described. While those figures are only my own estimates, I think they are about the average for houses in the range of $12,000.
There is also another group of workmen employed in the preparation of the site, installing the sewers, the water, gas, building of roadways and doing the landscaping. I relate these things to try to show how important house building is in our economy and how important it is to make mortgage money available at all times for builders who

build on speculation and for private citizens who wish to secure direct loans and handle their own contracts.
I would like to say a word with regard to private citizens who wish to secure direct loans and handle their own contracts and build under the supervision of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation inspectors. At one time much of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation building was done in this manner and was done by small building contractors who, among other construction work they did, built some four to six houses per year, what might be called custom built houses. There has been a tendency in recent years for all or most of the mortgage money to be taken up by the larger developers, with whom I have no quarrel. However, I do feel that the house building industry would be more stable if there were funds available at all times for the individual potential home owner so that he could secure a loan and build on land he may own or wish to purchase, not on a development subdivision. I do not say that that cannot be done at the present time; it can, but in recent years, when Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation money became available, it was taken up in a short time by the big developers, leaving long periods when no funds were available. I would recommend to the minister that he give consideration to setting aside a small block of mortgage funds for house building of the type I have tried to describe on a year round basis.
This kind of lending has certain advantages, first to the home owner. He can select his own site especially in the smaller communities; he can save the legal fees by having the loan in his own name from the start, thereby avoiding the title transfer. He can also eliminate real estate commission; he can have the house built by the builder of his choice at competitive prices and thereby save money. The small building contractor will also have many benefits. First of all, it would keep him in the house building business, which is most important. It has been noticed in the last few years that house building is drifting away from the small builder and going to the big subdivider. If loans of that class were available the year round it would firm up the business of the small building contractor; it would make it easier for him to provide year round employment to his workers. It would encourage him to take on young men as apprentices, which is something badly needed in Canada today.
I cannot express too strongly the need of keeping the small general contractors in the house building business. They employ mostly union workmen; they pay fair wages and
National Housing Act
they teach apprentices in the building trade, all of which is necessary and can best be done by making year round mortgage funds available for what I have described as custom built houses.
I do feel that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should do more by way of research in the development of low cost houses. It is true that one was developed last year, and while I have no figures on how popular it was, I do not think it was very popular. There is a great market for low cost housing, and everything should be done to promote it in areas where there is an acute housing need.
I have also been a great supporter of the land development schemes whereby the municipalities and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would purchase land, put in the services and make it available to house builders to buy in one or two lots. Land assembly scheme is the proper term to use. This is a scheme which should be pushed a little harder than it is being pushed at the present time.
In closing, I will not speak about apartment building, but I will say that I do favour subsidized slum clearance projects in the larger cities where the need for better housing is most acute for people in the low income group. There are a great many other things that could be said in connection with housing at this time, but I should like to leave an opportunity for others who may wish to go into other phases of the business. All I can say is that the setting aside of this money, as the Minister of Public Works is doing, is going to do a great service to the Canadian construction industry. It is going to create many jobs and it will also provide homes in many parts of Canada where they are badly needed.

Mr. Chairman, first I wish to extend my congratulations to the minister on his appointment as Minister of Public Works. He will certainly carry the good will and good wishes of all members and I am sure that if he adopts the patience which his efficient predecessor displayed he will undoubtedly fill the office with credit and distinction. That one of the first items of business of his administration to come before the house should be housing is a good omen and augurs well for many people who are in need of better accommodation which, without government assistance, their low incomes would not permit them to acquire.
There is considerable agitation in various parts of Canada at present for speedy action on slum clearance and for the rehousing of families who live on very low incomes. It has been recently reported that houses built during the last five years exceeded net family

The hon. member for Hamilton South made a very fine speech on housing on the closing day of the throne speech debate and, with the exception of some statements he made on which I have some reservations, I wholeheartedly agree with his observations and I wish to congratulate him on his contribution to this subject which, so far as I am concerned, is still one of the important factors in the welfare of the community. I was pleased to hear the hon. member say that there are 1,300 government rental projects in his riding with respect to which the government puts up 75 per cent of the cost of construction of the dwelling. The remaining 25 per cent is not all contributed by the provincial government as stated by the hon. member, but I am sure this was just an oversight on his part. The division is 17\ per cent contributed by the province and 7J per cent by the municipality. In passing may I also remind the hon. member that it was a Liberal government that introduced the legislation which made the 1,300 housing projects in his constituency possible.
In its long and distinguished record of achievement in the field of social legislation the former Liberal government established one of the most beneficial measures for the people of Canada in the low income group when it enacted the National Housing Act under which thousands of Canadians were provided with low rental homes who otherwise would have been forced to live in slum type dwellings. Several hundred homes were built in my own constituency of Fort William and I am still a very strong advocate of rental homes for those who cannot afford to buy.
The intent of the resolution does not cover spending for the construction of homes for rent under the National Housing Act, but if the government wishes to improve the act I strongly recommend an amendment which would provide for a federal share of 75 per cent and include the cost of water and sewer installations and the construction of sidewalks which at present are left to the hard-pressed municipalities which can hardly afford an additional outlay of money owing to the ever-increasing difficulties of borrowing.
With a population of approximately 18 million, an estimated 150,000 marriages will take place in Canada this year. These couples are all potential home owners. All will become tenants of houses or apartments, and the demand will increase as the population grows. It is true that in 1959 the number of marriages in Canada dropped to 127,000 but I am glad to say that the prospects for 1960 are much

brighter and perhaps closer to the figure I have mentioned. I now wish to quote from a submission I have received from the lake-head housebuilders association. I commend this submission to the minister as worthy of consideration. They say in part:
One of the largest industries at the lakehead is in grave danger of suffering a serious depression, with consequent curtailment of purchasing power and lay-offs of employees. We speak of the housing industry which has an annual turnover in the lake-head of approximately $15 million, of which approximately $7 million is paid out directly to the citizens of the lakehead cities in wages alone.
We commend the government, which in the past years, under the National Housing Act, has been responsible for a steady source of mortgage moneys, not only directly, but also through lending institutions, which have been influenced by the fact that the government guaranteed repayment. There is a desperate need for a stable source of mortgage funds, so that planning may commence prior to the actual period of construction which, as you are aware, is quite limited in the lakehead due to the weather problem.
Up until the end of 1959 in the lakehead cities, there were only three life insurance companies and one trust company financing new house construction under the National Housing Act, and then to only a limited degree. No other life insurance companies, trust companies and other lending institutions, will advance moneys in the lakehead area because they find that due to its isolated location and distance from their regional offices, the costs of administration are too high. Up to the end of 1959 for this reason, most lakehead housing projects have been financed directly through either Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or the banks. However, you can well appreciate that, in view of the fact that banks are limited to a maximum interest rate of 6 per cent and the National Housing Act's present rate is 6j per cent, there can be no hope held out for any real participation by the banks during the coming building season.
At this moment, there has been nothing done by the government in the way of indicating its program of lending under N.H.A. for 1960 and the three life insurance companies and one trust company which have loaned in the lakehead area have not yet committed themselves for one single loan.
One of the life insurance companies and the trust company have already stated that they will not be lending under the N.H.A. in 1960.
Local builders are receiving many inquiries from prospective purchasers who wish to build under the system which has been established in the last couple of years, but of course, no builder can give them any indication of what prospects they might have for obtaining financing. This, of course, leaves the builders and the prospective purchasers in a state of suspension. Unless the situation is soon resolved, many workmen temporarily laid off as a result of the curtailment of mortgage financing last October, simply will not be called back.
The letter goes on with more facts, but I see that time is limited and I will just leave that and proceed to the rest of my presentation. It is rather significant that the building volume in 1960 in most cities throughout Canada, including my own city of Fort William and the city of Ottawa, is the lowest since 1950. There are newcomers to be considered, and if immigrants are considered as well as the result
National Housing Act
of an adequate immigration policy being adopted, it will mean a greater demand for housebuilding than anticipated. In this event, even the estimated 125,000 new homes for 1960 may be short of meeting the demand. According to the Canadian Builder, a publication of the building industry, the battle for money is going to be fierce in 1960. I quote: House builders this year face the toughest battle for mortgage money ever fought in Canada.
It is obvious that the 60 per cent limit of appraisal value for conventional loans is not in step with present economic trends. It curtails too much the financial participation of the lender and makes too heavy a burden on the purchaser of a home. Thus, a potential purchaser must decide against buying or find someone who will make a loan on a second mortgage who, if found, invariably demands an excessively high rate of interest.
On Monday, March 7, I asked the minister the following question:
Would the minister consider doing away with the compulsory insurance feature on C.M.H.C. mortgages or at least reduce the insurance fee to a more reasonable figure in order to mitigate, to a slight degree, the crippling impact of this government's policy on the construction industry during 1960?
The following day the minister answered no. I believe it is time for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to drop the requirement which forces a home owner to insure the mortgage on his home. This is distinctly an added burden to the purchaser of the home and represents as much as $300 on present mortgages. It works in this way. The bank pays this fee to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and adds it on to the mortgage. In other words, the home owner not only has to pay an unnecessary fee, but he has to pay interest on it which, over the life of the mortgage if it be 30 years, will amount to something like $600.
It has been reported that in five years Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has accumulated $60 million from the mortgage insurance system, a scheme designed to protect the lender against default. However, the defaults have numbered less than 30 all told. In other words, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has collected $60 million in insurance premiums while payments to beneficiaries have totalled less than $300,000. It seems to me that this insurance scheme should be reduced by 75 per cent at least, if not removed entirely. The removal of this premium could stimulate the industry which, when properly organized, is a stabilizing factor in employment because there is no other industry of which I know that spreads the benefits of employment more evenly in the economy of a community.

If houses are not selling, it is not because there are no customers but because the down payment is too high. I should like to illustrate what I mean by citing what happened in the town of Atikokan, 130 miles west of Fort William and which is on the fringe of my constituency. On January 7 the weekly town newspaper carried an advertisement offering 20 new homes for sale at down payments of $500 instead of the usual $2,000 to $3,000. Within five days 18 of the homes had been sold. This is irrefutable evidence that Canadians everywhere are anxious to own their own homes. People close to the scene have made the statement that not more than one or two of these 20 homes would have been sold if as much as $2,000 had been required as a down payment. Past experience has proven that such high down payments just cannot be met by young couples trying to give their children a decent standard of living while still paying for furniture and other appliances.
What Canada needs today is a move toward lower building costs, better mortgage arrangements and more realistic building standards in housing. I submit that the government would do well to sponsor a national competition for a design and specifications for a home that the great majority of Canadians could afford. This might uncover a new design acceptable to Canadian conditions. The cost of such an undertaking would be small and the benefits to the national economy would be great. I urge the minister to give these suggestions serious consideration.
Progress reported.
